title: Your LLM Stack Is a 2008 Database With Better Marketing — Lovina Dmello, NVIDIA
talk_summary: A security-focused talk arguing that production ML failures are mostly boring infrastructure misconfigurations (over-privileged access, flat networks, exposed secrets) rather than exotic adversarial attacks, and that defenses must be deployed with acceptable latency overhead. It offers a maturity model and a short list of hygiene fixes rather than novel techniques.

takeaways.what_they_do: Audit found default setups give every account full admin rights with non-expiring credentials; fix is each account does only what it needs and credentials expire quickly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: each account like should do only what it needs to do. And then the credentials to should expire very quickly.
takeaways.numbers: 78% of 50 audited production ML setups had at least one critical security mistake

takeaways.technique: Segment agent/build network from control plane
takeaways.what_they_do: Flat networks let an attacker who enters one part reach everything; fix is walling parts off and requiring verified identity between services, not just network access.
takeaways.evidence_quote: nothing stops one part of the system from reaching another part of the system

takeaways.technique: Secret scanning + secret manager before ship
takeaways.what_they_do: Passwords hardcoded in code and model files in open storage are common; fix is a secret manager, encryption, and automatic scanning before shipping.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a proper secret manager, encryption, and automatic scanning before before all of this ships

takeaways.what_they_do: Cheap basics (auth, input checks) cost <8% and should always run; heavier isolation 10-20% used selectively; expensive real-time malicious-input detection 15-30% only on high-risk paths.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the cheap controls everywhere and we can save the expensive ones for the heavier risk systems

takeaways.technique: Maturity self-assessment against a fixed checklist
takeaways.what_they_do: Use a 4-level maturity model tied to overhead budget to locate where you actually stand, since most teams believe they're at level 3 but are at 1-2.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most of teams teams believe that they are at level three, but uh they are actually either at level one or two
